title: Quantification of microglial contact and engulfment of oligodendrocyte progenitor cells in the rodent brain
protocol: Place dry slide on the stage of the confocal microscope.
Locate the area of interest, such as the corpus callosum at the level of the lateral ventricles in a coronal section.
Focus on one region within the area of interest using a high-powered objective.
Set the laser power and gain for each wavelength to optimize the image without overexposure.
Optimize laser power and gain settings on a non-essential region of the tissue before imaging.
Set the top and bottom of the z-stack based on cell clarity in the image.
Ensure the z-stack thickness is 15 μm.
Set the step size to 0.3 μm.
Test microscope settings on an unnecessary section to avoid photobleaching.
Keep laser power low and adjust gain for increased brightness.
Image three regions of the corpus callosum as indicated.
Acquire z-stacks in necessary color channels.
Capture a representative z-stack image.
Suggest imaging at least 2–3 brain sections per mouse.
Start imaging on one end of the area of interest and work across to avoid repeating regions.
Ensure all image stacks are uniform in size across x, y, and z planes.
Image live cells or ex vivo slices using time-lapse confocal microscopy as alternatives.
Begin data analysis after acquiring images; keep slides at 4°C for long-term storage.
Prepare image stacks for import into Imaris software according to the specific imaging timing required (∼15 min per stack).
Check the latest version of Imaris for supported file formats and system requirements.
Import image stacks into the Imaris software Arena.
Open Imaris and click the Image button to import an image or folder into the arena.
Drag images directly into the arena for import.
Ensure the status bar on the bottom right corner displays file import progress.
Double-click the file of interest in the arena to open it.
Click the “3D View” icon from the menu to view the image stack in 3D.
Rotate the image using the “Navigate” tool.
Adjust display settings using the “Display Adjustment” window.
Show the “Display Adjustment” window by clicking “Edit” and selecting “Show Display Adjustment.”
Adjust colors of the image for accessibility under “Image Properties…”
Process images for noise using smoothing functions under the “Image Processing” tab.
Create a surface render for microglia in the FITC channel.
Deselect all channels except FITC in the “Display Adjustment” window.
Click the “Add New Surfaces” icon within the “Scene” window.
Rename the new line within the “Scene” folder to “Microglia.”
Navigate to the menu below with the tab “Create” selected by default.
Ensure that the “Segment a Region of Interest” button is not selected.
Click the blue arrow button on the bottom to advance to the next step.
Select the FITC channel for surface rendering.
Adjust smoothing to 0.1 μm.
Threshold the image using the histogram.
Do not enable the “Split Touching Objects” option.
Check thresholding by zooming in on the cells.
Rotate cells around to ensure boundary accuracy.
Process all tissue samples at the same time.
Use consistent microscope acquisition settings for all samples within an experiment.
Determine threshold settings in a small representative pilot sample.
Apply determined threshold settings consistently throughout experimental image stacks.
Ensure thresholding covers 100% of the cell boundary.
Analyze data in a blinded and unbiased manner.
Return to the default view of the image by clicking the “Reset” button.
Click the blue arrow to advance to the next step once satisfied with the thresholding.
Select the microglia surface render in the “Scene” window.
Click the “Color” button within the bottom menu and change the “Color Type” to “Object ID”.
Use the “Navigate” feature of the pointer to move around the image.
Switch between the “Navigate” and “Select” features using the “Esc” key or by clicking the buttons.
Edit individual objects in the surface render.
Delete objects which are not cells based on no nuclear staining.
Merge separated cell objects using the “Unify” feature.
Split clustered cells within one object to separate them.
To zoom in and out of an area, scroll the mouse while the pointer is set to "Navigate."
Change the selection box size by scrolling the mouse while the pointer is set to "Select."
Move from one side of the image to the other to review all cells.
Merge or separate objects as needed during navigation.
Right-click and drag the image to move to a new field within the image while in "Navigate" mode.
Continuously turn the surface render on and off to view the raw image by clicking the checkbox next to the "Microglia" surface within the "Scene" window.
Use a nuclear stain such as bisbenzimide in the DAPI channel to identify cells.
Turn channels on and off within the "Display Adjustment" window for better visualization.
Select the first object using the "Select" mode.
Hold the "Ctrl" key and click additional objects that need to be merged together.
Objects should turn yellow as they are selected.
Click the "Unify" button under the “Editing” window once all needed areas are selected.
The objects should turn the same color indicating they are now one object.
Be sure that the “Edit” menu is selected for separating two objects.
Use the nuclear stain to identify individual cells and determine where the cut needs to be made.
Orient the object using the "Navigate" feature of the pointer to allow a vertical line cut.
Switch the pointer to “Select” mode once the object is correctly positioned for cutting.
Hold down the “Shift” key, then click the object to indicate the cut location.
A line should appear indicating where it will be cut.
If the line is not appropriate, click the "Clear Scissor" button on the editing tab.
Move the object back into position using the "Navigate" feature of the pointer.
Create a new vertical cut by switching back to “Select” mode and clicking the correct area while holding the “Shift” key.
Set the pointer to “Select”.
Click on an artifact object to select it.
Click the “Delete” button under the edit menu for the surface render.
Check parameters for an individual object before deleting by clicking the “Statistics” button.
Select “Detailed” from the dropdown menu to choose various parameters such as volume or sphericity.
Set parameters for objects that should be excluded based on volume or sphericity.
Delete all objects below a specified threshold, such as 10 μm3.
Create a surface render for OPCs in the TRITC channel.
Deselect the surface render of microglia under the “Scene” window.
Deselect the FITC channel from appearing with the “Display Adjustment” window.
Select the TRITC channel instead to show the OPCs.
Click the “Add New Surfaces” icon within the “Scene” window.
Rename the new line in the “Scene” folder to “OPCs.”
Navigate to the menu with the tab “Create” selected and click the blue arrow button.
Select the TRITC channel in the “Source Channel” step.
Set the smoothing setting for OPCs to 0.4 μm.
Use absolute thresholding for this protocol.
Click the blue arrow to advance to the next step.
Threshold the image until the gray surface accurately represents the cells.
Click the blue arrow to advance to the next step.
Apply a filter with “Number of Voxels” set to 10 to remove small particles.
Click the green double arrow button to complete the surface render for OPCs.
Check or uncheck the checkbox for OPCs under the “Scene” window as needed.
To view both microglia and OPC surface renders together, check the “Microglia” surface render under the “Scene” window.
Manually edit the 3D surface render to accurately represent individual cells.
Ensure all cells are individual objects that colocalize with bisbenzimide, a marker of cell nuclei.
Filter out any surfaces with a volume less than 10 μm³ and sphericity value lower than 0.49 to exclude pericytes on blood vessels expressing the NG2 marker.
Select the “OPCs” surface render in the “Scene” window.
Click the “Color” button within the menu as shown by a rainbow hexagon.
Change the “Color Type” to “Object ID” to view objects in separate colors.
Navigate through the image to merge or separate objects.
Label each cell with a different color to indicate separate objects.
Ensure each individual cell is only one color, indicating it is a single object.
Exclude blood vessels when using NG2 as a marker for OPCs in transgenic mice or through immunostaining.
Sort all objects by volume from smallest to largest within the “Statistics” menu under “Detailed view.”
Select and delete all objects with a volume of 10 μm³ or less.
Sort the remaining objects by sphericity from smallest to largest within the same menu.
Delete all objects with a sphericity less than 0.49.
Identify internalized surfaces.
Determine what volume is internalized using the Surface-Surface Coloc XTension in Imaris.
Create a new 3D surface render of the internalized material with volume information.
Categorize OPCs that are being engulfed as having more than 15% of their cell volume internalized.
Categorize OPCs that are contacted but not engulfed as having less than 15% of their cell volume internalized.
Spot-check analyzed data to ensure cells are appropriately categorized.
Remove particles and objects fitting the exclusion criteria to avoid false categorizations.
Create a Random Color Map on the TRITC channel.
With the OPCs surface render selected, click the “Edit” tab.
Click the “Mask All…” button.
Choose the TRITC channel and click “Random Color Map.”
Select the “Duplicate channel before applying mask” checkbox.
Click “OK” to create a new masked TRITC channel with rainbow colors.
Create a new surface render of the internalized material within microglia.
Click the “Tools” tab within the OPCs surface render menu.
Click the “Surface-Surface coloc” link on the list.
Select the two surfaces to colocalize (Microglia and OPCs).
Click continue.
Do not use the smoothing feature for this protocol.
View “ColocChannel” in a gray gradient color within the “Display Adjustment” window.
Identify new objects representing the internalized area of OPCs within microglia.
Select “ColocSurface” from the “Scene” window to view individual surface renders.
Click checkboxes to select and view each render individually or merged together.
Identify regions on the OPCs that have a large volume internalized by viewing surfaces separately and together.
Store the file at any time to save edited surface renders.
Create surface renders on all files before proceeding with data analysis.
Obtain 3D Surface Renders for all cells.
Generate a separate 3D Surface Render for the internalized portion of OPCs.
Select the ColocSurface render representing the voxels labeled in both OPC and microglia surface volumes that come in contact with each other.
Calculate the volume from the ColocSurface render.
Obtain the total volume from the OPCs.
Divide the volume from the ColocSurface render by the volume from the OPCs to determine internalization amount.
Select the ColocSurface render in the “Scene” menu.
Click the “Statistics” tab (denoted by a graph icon) in the window of the bottom left corner of the screen.
Choose “Detailed” view within the Statistics tab.
Select “Volume” from the second drop-down menu to display volumes of each ColocSurface render.
Export statistics by clicking “Export Statistics on Tab Display to File” (save icon).
Delete any surface that is less than 1 μm³ to avoid particles.
Export data by clicking the "Export Statistics on Tab Display to File" button.
Save exported data as a .csv file and open in Excel.
Resave the data as an Excel Workbook (.xlsx) format if needed.
Calculate the percent internalization by dividing the internalized surface volume (ColocSurface) by the total volume of the OPC.
Manually enter the volume for the OPC that the ColocSurface corresponds with in new columns within the Excel sheet.
Set up a new column to divide the internalized volume by the total OPC volume to calculate percent internalization.
Create a new section of columns to input parameters for the OPC corresponding to the ColocSurface volume, including OPC ID, volume, and percent internalization.
Organize the ColocSurface render volume data by ID from smallest to largest within the Imaris software.
Click the first object of the ColocSurface render.
Ensure its volume matches the volume in the data file for that ID.
Turn on the surface render for the OPCs to view the cell corresponding to this volume.
Click the OPC to determine its volume and ID.
Enter the information within the data sheet to correspond with the appropriate ColocSurface ID.
Calculate percent internalization by dividing the ColocSurface volume by the OPC volume.
Set the format of the percent internalization column to percentage by right-clicking the column, then “Format Cells…” and select “Percentage,” then click “OK.”
Continue through each ColocSurface volume and match it with the appropriate OPC surface render.
Enter the data as directed in the above steps until the data sheet is complete.
